newsitem.title: UK: New British Conservative Party leader seen by July.
newsitem.headline: New British Conservative Party leader seen by July.

text.p: Conservative chairman Brian Mawhinney said on Monday he expected a new party leader to be picked by July, adding he hoped the contest would not widen internal splits over policy on Britain's relations with the European Union.

"I would expect the new leader to be in office, with a new team, certainly before the end of June," he told BBC radio, four days after his party was routed in a general election after 18 unbroken years of rule.

Following the Conservatives' crushing defeat by the Labour party, John Major, who had been prime minister for 6-1/2 years, said he would resign as party leader and make way for someone who could heal the divisions over Europe and lead the party back to power.
Mawhinney expressed hope that potential candidates -- so far only two men have formally put their names forward -- would offer themselves up with the goal of renewing and improving the party.
Asked if the race could worsen the party's acrimonious infighting over Britain's ties with the EU, he replied: "I certainly hope that it isn't going to polarise (the situation)."
"We had a very bad result last Thursday night. We need to reflect on that. We need to analyse why, ensure that there are changes," said Mawhinney.
The Conservatives faced five years until their next shot at winning power and the party must use the time wisely, he said.
"We're talking about a general election in the next millennium, so I'm hoping that my colleagues will reflect, that they will analyse, that they will think first and talk afterwards."
Former finance minister Kenneth Clarke, a leading pro-European, was the first to recover from the election debacle and declare himself a candidate to succeed Major.
But since well over half of the remaining 165 Conservative MPs consider themselves Eurosceptic, Clarke's strong credentials on paper might not appeal to many of his party colleagues.

On the other side of the political spectrum, right-wing Eurosceptic Peter Lilley, another former cabinet minister, has joined the race and John Redwood, who stood against Major for the leadership in 1995, is almost certain to throw in his hat.
Other potential candidates include former health minister Stephen Dorell and William Hague, the 36-year-old former Welsh secretary.

Major, who has laid low since his election defeat, was due to hold meetings this week to discuss plugging the gaps in his top team of advisers, gutted by the loss of several key ministers at the election.
The leadership contest itself is not expected before mid-June.
